feature: The reference edit every video speed fix measures against
summary: A long, busy video edit built the same way every time, at 6, 20 and 60 minutes: Retina screen recordings cut onto three picture tracks over a moving background, 37 cuts in every six minutes with dissolves, pushes, cubes and flips, titles, zooms, sound and music. One command opens it in the probe, and a walk can start with it open.
setup: The probe (Photonz Probe), release Next, no flag changed from its default. Nothing in the app changed for a person; this is a measuring tool.

try.do: Run Scripts/perf/reference-edit.sh 6. The first run on a Mac writes the recordings, about three minutes; after that it takes seconds.
Look at the timeline: Title, V2 with b-roll, V1 with the cuts and their transitions, zoom rows, and below them the background and music tracks.
Look at the contact sheet: twelve moments, among them the middle of a dissolve, a push, a cube and a flip.
Press Space, watch for three seconds, press Space again.
Run Scripts/perf/reference-edit.sh 20, then 60, and see how long each takes to become usable.

evaluate: Does the 6 minute edit look like a real screen-recording edit you would make, busy enough to be a fair test?
Is anything you do in your own edits missing from it (captions, speed changes, a second sound track, a freeze)?
Are 20 and 60 minutes the right long lengths to hold the app to?
rough: Playback on it is bad today, which is what it exists to show: at 1x the picture fell up to 124 frames behind the playhead, and the main thread froze for up to 4.3 s in one pass, the first about 0.3 s in. The speed tasks own this (a-speed-walk-measures-the-long-reference-edit-th, a-long-edit-with-transitions-plays-scrubs-and-ed).
Opening the 20 minute edit freezes the app for about 14 s and the 60 minute one for over two minutes, so the 60 minute walk ran out of time; filed as an-hour-long-edit-opens-in-a-few-seconds-not-two.
The walk claims only that Space starts and stops playback, not how far the playhead gets: it reached 4.7 s after a 3 s wait in one run and 0.37 s in another.

The recordings are drawn shapes and nonsense words standing in for real apps, at 60 fps H.264 with a voice-like buzz rather than speech; what they give the decoder (big flat areas, sharp text, a few things moving) is what a screen recording gives it.
The contact sheet is drawn by the renderer from frames read off the recordings, the way an export draws them, not photographed from the window.
No mock covers this: it is a tool, not a surface.
